prompt: Why is "is self-hosting cheaper than an API?" a utilisation question rather than a price comparison?
answer_markdown: The two options are billed in different units: a GPU is billed by the hour whether it produces one token or a million, while an API is billed per token. To compare them you must convert the hourly rate into a per-token rate, and that conversion divides by how many tokens you actually produced in the hour — which is throughput multiplied by utilisation. Utilisation therefore sits alone in the denominator and scales the answer linearly: the identical GPU serving the identical model costs ten times as much per token at 10% utilisation as at 100%. Because no other variable in the model has that leverage, the decision reduces to whether you can keep the hardware busy, not to whose sticker price is lower. This is also why comparing an hourly GPU rate directly against a per-million-token API price — the most common version of this mistake — produces wildly optimistic "10x cheaper" claims.

prompt: Work through the break-even calculation for a $2.20/hour GPU achieving 2,500 tokens/second against an API at $0.50 per million tokens. Then say what changes when you add a second replica for availability and 20 monthly hours of ops at $90/hour.
answer_markdown: At full tilt the GPU produces 2,500 x 3,600 = 9 million tokens per hour, so $2.20 / 9 million works out to roughly $0.24 per million tokens — under half the API's $0.50, which looks decisive. But that assumes 100% utilisation. The break-even utilisation is the point where the self-hosted cost per million equals the API's: monthly fixed cost is $2.20 x 730 = $1,606, full-tilt monthly output is 9 million x 730 = 6.57 billion tokens, and solving $1,606 / (6.57e9 x u) x 1e6 = $0.50 gives u of about 48.9%. Now add reality: two replicas doubles the fixed cost to $3,212 while also doubling full-tilt output, and 20 ops hours at $90 adds $1,800 that produces no tokens at all — pushing the break-even to about 76.3%. The lesson is that the naive figure understates the bar by more than half, and sustaining 76% average utilisation on traffic with nights and weekends is genuinely hard. All figures are illustrative and should be re-derived from current prices.

prompt: Which costs do teams most often leave out of a self-hosting business case?
answer_markdown: Engineer time is both the largest omission and the largest line item at small scale — at a loaded hourly rate, one engineer spending a quarter of their week on serving infrastructure costs more per month than several GPUs, and it appears in no spreadsheet. On-call is next: someone must answer when a driver wedges or a node fails at 3 a.m. Redundancy is the one that quietly breaks the arithmetic, because a single GPU is not a production deployment — every restart, node upgrade and hardware fault becomes an outage — so realistic sizing is at least two replicas, doubling the fixed cost before serving a single extra token. Then there is evaluation infrastructure, which an API vendor effectively provides by testing their own models, and model upgrades: a vendor ships an improved model and you get it, whereas self-hosted every upgrade is a re-benchmark, re-evaluate and re-deploy project. Because these all sit in the same numerator as the GPU rate, they raise the break-even utilisation exactly as more expensive hardware would.

prompt: Name reasons to self-host that have nothing to do with cost, and reasons to use an API even at high volume.
answer_markdown: Some requirements override the arithmetic entirely and are worth raising before being asked. Towards self-hosting: data residency or regulation that forbids sending data to a third-party processor, which can make an API simply illegal for the use case; a contractual no-subprocessors commitment to your own customers; predictable latency free of a vendor's shared multi-tenant queue and rate limits; and needing a fine-tuned model or one no vendor hosts. Towards the API despite high volume: traffic that is bursty enough that you would pay for large amounts of idle GPU, a small team with no capacity to run infrastructure and an on-call rotation, fast-moving model requirements where you want each vendor upgrade for free, and needing frontier capability, which you cannot self-host at any price. Naming both directions is what distinguishes a considered answer from an ideological one.

prompt: In an interview, why is a confident single break-even number a weaker answer than a model with a stated range?
answer_markdown: Because the number will be wrong and the model will not. The break-even depends on measured throughput on your own traffic shape, on achievable utilisation, on how many replicas availability requires, and on how much ops burden you count — and reasonable people will disagree about each. A single number hides which of those assumptions you made, so the interviewer cannot tell whether you understood the sensitivity or just multiplied whatever figures you remembered. Stating the model explicitly, then the range it produces, and then what would flip the answer shows you know which variables dominate: throughput and utilisation each move the result by multiples, while the GPU hourly rate moves it only linearly. It also makes the conversation productive, because a disagreeing interviewer corrects one of your inputs rather than dismissing your reasoning — the same discipline that makes back-of-envelope capacity estimates defensible.

prompt: You calculated a 49% break-even utilisation and self-hosting looked good. Then you measure real throughput at 900 tokens/second instead of the 2,500 you assumed. What happens, and what does it tell you about which variables matter?
answer_markdown: The break-even moves from about 49% to roughly 136%, which means it is unachievable at any utilisation — self-hosting cannot win on cost for this workload no matter how well you pack the hardware. Nothing about the price or the card changed; only the measured throughput did, and it moved the answer by a factor of nearly three. That establishes the sensitivity ranking: achievable throughput and utilisation each shift the result by multiples, while the hourly rate shifts it linearly, so a 45% cheaper instance improves your position by 45% but cannot rescue a workload that is off by 3x. It also explains why benchmark numbers are dangerous inputs — real throughput depends on prompt and output lengths, batch size, quantisation, and how much VRAM is left for the KV cache after weights, so a vendor figure measured on short prompts in large batches can be several times what your traffic achieves. The two questions that decide the whole decision are what throughput you actually get and how full you can keep it.
